name: llms.txt Proposal
definition: llms.txt is a proposal for providing a concise Markdown overview that helps AI agents find and use a website's content. The file can summarize a site or section, explain important context, and link to relevant resources.
sources: Jeremy Howard: The llms.txt Proposal, v2 (https://llmstxt.org/)
Google Search Central: AI Features and Your Website (https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features)
contentMarkdown:
# llms.txt Proposal

llms.txt is a proposal for providing a concise Markdown overview that helps AI agents find and use a website's content. The file can summarize a site or section, explain important context, and link to relevant resources.

It is a community proposal rather than a universal requirement for AI systems or search engines. Whether an agent reads it depends on that agent's behavior.

## What the file contains

The proposal specifies a project or site name as an H1, with optional summary text, explanatory content, and sections of descriptive links. Its current version permits files at the site root or within a section, such as a documentation directory.

It also recommends clean Markdown versions of relevant pages and link relations that help clients discover those versions.

## Example: a product design glossary

A glossary could provide a short explanation of its scope and grouped links to core terms, such as OOUX, accessibility, and design tokens. Each link description should explain what information is available.

If Markdown page versions are offered, keep them synchronized with the public articles. A stale summary or broken link can make the file less useful.

## Does llms.txt improve SEO?

Google states that no new AI text files or special schema.org markup are required for inclusion in AI Overviews or AI Mode. Publishing llms.txt does not guarantee indexing, ranking improvements, or citations.

For a small site, consider it an optional documentation experiment. First maintain useful visible content, discoverable internal links, and correct indexing controls.

If implemented, test whether agents can answer representative questions using the file and its links. Review actual usage where observable rather than assuming a search benefit.

name: Multimodal AI
definition: Multimodal AI processes or combines information in more than one modality, such as text, images, audio, or video. A multimodal system might answer a written question about a photo or use a spoken request together with information shown on a screen.

contentMarkdown:
# Multimodal AI

Multimodal AI processes or combines information in more than one modality, such as text, images, audio, or video. A multimodal system might answer a written question about a photo or use a spoken request together with information shown on a screen.

## What can multimodal AI do?

| Input | Example output |
|---|---|
| A receipt image and a written instruction | A draft expense entry with the merchant, date, currency, and amount. |
| An audio recording and a request for a summary | A written account of the discussion and proposed action items. |
| A screenshot and a written question | An explanation of a visible interface state. |

The supported combinations depend on the model and the application. Check which inputs and outputs the chosen system accepts and evaluate the task you intend to support.

## How does multimodal AI relate to generative AI?

Multimodal describes the types of information a system handles. Generative AI creates content. A system that reads a receipt image and generates a written explanation uses both capabilities. Other multimodal applications may classify content or retrieve matching items.

## Example: Reviewing a receipt in an expense app

An employee uploads a receipt and asks the app to prepare an expense entry. The system sends the image and instructions to a model that supports image input. It presents the extracted fields beside the source image so the employee can correct them before submitting.

Test the flow with blurred images, different layouts, and receipts showing several totals or currencies. Check whether the app identifies missing or ambiguous information and lets the employee resolve it. Measure field correctness and successful submission, including whether the saved amount and currency match the intended expense.

name: Knowledge Graphs (AI Context)
definition: A knowledge graph represents entities and the relationships between them in a graph structure, often with properties and identifiers. In AI applications, it can supply structured context for retrieval, reasoning, and explanation.
contentMarkdown:
# Knowledge Graphs (AI Context)

A knowledge graph represents entities and the relationships between them in a graph structure, often with properties and identifiers. In AI applications, it can supply structured context for retrieval, reasoning, and explanation.

For example, a graph can connect a hotel to its rooms, a reservation to its guest, and a maintenance issue to the room it affects. Relationships make those connections available for queries.

## Example: finding affected reservations

Suppose room 204 has an unresolved maintenance issue. A hotel tool could follow relationships from that room to overlapping reservations and their assigned guests.

An AI assistant could use the resulting records to explain which reservations need review. The application still needs date logic, current data, and access checks to determine the actual result.

Stable identifiers matter: two guests with the same name should remain distinct entities. Record where important facts came from and when they were updated.

## Knowledge graphs and RAG

A knowledge graph can support retrieval-augmented generation by helping retrieve connected facts. Graphs can also be combined with keyword or vector search.

Microsoft's GraphRAG is one specific approach that builds a graph and community summaries from text. Its architecture does not define every graph-based retrieval system.

RDF is one way to represent graph data; knowledge graphs can also use other data models.

## Check the relationships

Define the meaning and direction of each relationship. Validate extracted entities, duplicate records, and unsupported connections before relying on them.

A graph structures information, including information that may be incomplete or incorrect. Test retrieval quality and the generated answer against the underlying sources. More connections alone do not establish better answers.

## Related terms

- [Conceptual Schema](/glossary/conceptual-schema.html)
- [Domain Context Modeling](/glossary/domain-context-modeling.html)
- [Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)](/glossary/retrieval-augmented-generation-rag.html)
- [Structured Data for LLMs](/glossary/structured-data-for-llms.html)

## Sources

name: Agentic UX
definition: Agentic UX is the design of experiences in which people delegate goals or tasks to AI agents and retain appropriate visibility and control over the work. It covers the interaction before, during, and after an agent takes action.
sources: Google PAIR: Errors and Graceful Failure (https://pair.withgoogle.com/chapter/errors-failing/)
contentMarkdown:
# Agentic UX

Agentic UX is the design of experiences in which people delegate goals or tasks to AI agents and retain appropriate visibility and control over the work. It covers the interaction before, during, and after an agent takes action.

A conversational interface is one possible entry point. The experience may also include task queues, approval screens, notifications, and activity records.

## Example: updating a set of reservations

An operations manager asks an agent to find reservations affected by a schedule change and prepare customer notifications.

Before work begins, the interface makes the affected date range and intended actions visible. During the task, it distinguishes records being checked from messages awaiting review. Before sending, it lets the manager inspect recipients, content, and exceptions.

If some messages fail, the final state identifies which were sent, which failed, and which have an uncertain outcome. The recovery path should avoid sending successful messages again.

## Design around delegation

Useful questions include:

- What information does the agent need before starting?
- Which actions are already authorized?
- Where can a person inspect, change, or stop the work?
- What happens to completed actions when the task stops?
- How does the user resolve missing information or partial failure?

A stop control needs an accurate explanation of its effect. It may prevent further work without reversing changes already made.

## Evaluate the outcome

Test whether users can understand what happened and take the next appropriate action. Include unexpected results and delayed approvals.

Keep necessary review concise and informative. Approval is useful when the reviewer can identify the target, proposed change, and consequence.

## Related terms

- [Human-in-the-Loop (HITL)](/glossary/human-in-the-loop-hitl.html)
- [Operational UX](/glossary/operational-ux.html)
- [AI-native Design](/glossary/ai-native-design.html)
- [Agent Harness](/glossary/agent-harness.html)

- [Conversational UX](/glossary/conversational-ux.html)

name: System Prompts & Guardrails
definition: System prompts provide application-level instructions that guide an AI model’s behavior. Guardrails are additional controls that check or constrain inputs, outputs, and actions around the model. Together they help define how an AI feature is expected to operate.
sources: Prompt Injection, OWASP Gen AI Security Project (https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/)
contentMarkdown:
# System Prompts & Guardrails

System prompts provide application-level instructions that guide an AI model’s behavior. Guardrails are additional controls that check or constrain inputs, outputs, and actions around the model. Together they help define how an AI feature is expected to operate.

## What belongs in each layer?

A prompt can explain the assistant’s role, response format, and how to handle missing information. Application controls can validate structured output, restrict available tools, check authorization, and pause an operation for review.

The system should enforce permissions at the point where an action is executed. Retrieved text and model output can contain misleading instructions, so the application needs a defined way to handle them.

## Example: Preparing a flight change

A booking assistant is instructed to explain available options and identify uncertain conditions. Its tools can retrieve a booking and prepare a quote. The application checks that the requesting user can access the booking and that the quote is still current.

Before executing the change, the workflow presents the proposed itinerary and price for approval. The execution service validates the approved operation and returns its actual result.

## How do you evaluate the controls?

Test ordinary requests, malformed outputs, stale quotes, unauthorized records, and retrieved text that tries to redirect the assistant. Check the behavior of the complete workflow, including what the user sees when a check fails. Record whether the controls prevented the invalid action and whether the user could recover.

## Related terms

- [Context Engineering](/glossary/context-engineering.html)
- [Agent Harness](/glossary/agent-harness.html)
- [Design Harness](/glossary/design-harness.html)
- [Prompt Engineering](/glossary/prompt-engineering.html)

- [Prompt Injection](/glossary/prompt-injection.html)
